title: Self-Rewarding and Meta-Rewarding: When the Judge Is the Student

questions.question: Why does the Self-Rewarding paper (Yuan et al. 2024) argue that the policy should be its own reward model?
options: Because DPO cannot consume scores from a separately trained reward model, so the policy has to emit its own
Because human preference data becomes too expensive to collect once the policy is larger than about 70B parameters
Because a reward model trained on human preferences is capped at human level and stays frozen while the policy improves
Because judging with a rubric is an easier task than generating, so a model judging itself is always reliable
questions.explanation: The paper's motivation is that a human-trained reward model is bottlenecked by human performance and frozen during training; letting the model judge gives a reward signal that can keep improving. The other options are not claims the paper makes.

questions.question: Which pair of paper-reported facts from Yuan et al. together motivates this lesson's worry about self-rewarding loops?
options: AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate rose 9.94% → 20.44% while mean response length rose 1,092 → 2,552 characters
Judge pairwise accuracy fell 81.7% → 65.1% while the number of preference pairs doubled each iteration
The model beat GPT-4 0613 on AlpacaEval while the EFT seed set shrank from 3,964 to 429 examples
DPO loss reached zero by iteration 2 while the actor stopped producing distinct candidates per prompt
questions.explanation: The win rate doubled and the responses more than doubled in length over three iterations; the paper itself says length may be a factor in relative performance. Judge accuracy actually rose (65.1% → 81.7%), and the other options invent numbers.

questions.question: Why does the judge in a Self-Rewarding loop saturate even though the shared weights keep being updated?
options: The KL penalty in DPO stops the judging behaviour from receiving any gradient after the first iteration, so it cannot change
The additive 0–5 rubric has only six distinct values, so the judge cannot express finer preferences once answers are decent
The EFT seed set is relabelled by the actor every iteration, so the judge's training targets keep moving under it
Nothing corrects the judge's own errors, so as candidates cluster near the top the remaining score gaps are mostly its biases
questions.explanation: After M1 the judge changes only incidentally through actor-pair DPO; no signal tells it which preferences were wrong. As candidates improve, ties get discarded and the surviving differences are the judge's biases (length, style), which the actor then learns.

questions.question: Which statement about Meta-Rewarding's length-control mechanism (Wu et al. 2024) is correct?
options: It is learned by the meta-judge from judgement pairs, so no human input is needed to decide what counts as too long
It is a hand-written selection rule: choose the shortest high-scoring candidate and reject the longest low-scoring one within ρ-bands
It truncates every response to 1,000 characters before judging, which is why length-controlled win rate is reported instead of raw
It penalizes the judge's score linearly in length, with the slope ρ fitted on AlpacaEval's length-controlled regression
questions.explanation: The chosen response is the shortest one with score in [(1−ρ)S_max + ρS_min, S_max] and the rejected one the longest with score in [S_min, (1−ρ)S_min + ρS_max]. It is a human-inserted constraint, not something the meta-judge learns.

questions.question: Your self-rewarding loop reports that judge agreement with GPT-4 on its own chosen pairs rose from 61% to 79% over four iterations. What do you need before trusting the judge?
options: Agreement with human labels on a fixed audit set the loop never trained on, re-scored by the current judge each iteration
A second run of the same loop with a different random seed, to show the agreement rise is not a random fluctuation
A higher agreement threshold, say 90%, since 79% still leaves too many pairs where the judge and GPT-4 disagree
A larger pool of candidates per prompt, since N = 4 produces too few pairs for the judge to be evaluated reliably
questions.explanation: Agreement on the loop's own pairs measures the judge against itself on a drifting distribution; Wu et al.'s human-agreement Spearman barely moved (0.315 → 0.326). Only a fixed, external, human-labelled set is a grounded signal.

questions.question: Why does adding a meta-meta-judge built from the same weights not answer the question 'who evaluates the evaluator'?
options: Because each extra judging layer multiplies inference cost by the number of judge samples, which no training budget can sustain
Because Elo fitting on pairwise judgements becomes numerically unstable once there are more than two layers of comparisons
Because DPO can only train one kind of preference per iteration, so judge pairs and meta-judge pairs cannot be mixed together
Because layers sharing the same weights share the same biases, so their errors correlate rather than cancel; something grounded must enter
questions.explanation: Stacking evaluators made of the same model correlates their errors (Wu et al. had to length-filter judgement pairs too). A meta-judge helps only when it has information the judge lacks, such as a fixed human-labelled audit set.
